rulings.sentence: **`workbench`** is the full application UI: parts such as the sidebar, panel, and status bar, plus the contributions, services, and features built on them.
The full application UI and its features. ... `workbench/browser` holds the layout and parts.
The full IDE shell: parts (editor area, sidebar, panel), `services/`, `contrib/` features, and `api/` (the extension host and the VS Code API implementation).
Some layers also have other environment folders, such as `electron-utility` or `server`. They follow the same pattern.

`workbench.desktop.main.ts` adds the `electron-sandbox` and node-backed pieces.
`workbench.common.main.ts` imports the contributions and services both builds share.
Contributions under `workbench/contrib/<feature>/` register themselves through side-effect imports, such as `import './contrib/foo/browser/foo.contribution.js'`.
Features are usually pulled in by side-effect imports of their `*.contribution.ts` files, which are listed in these entry points.
Each platform adds its own entry file on top: `workbench.desktop.main.ts` or `workbench.web.main.ts`.
A contribution that needs a service with no web implementation either gets a web stub or stays out of the web entry.
Contributions register themselves when their module runs (`registerWorkbenchContribution2`, `registerSingleton`, `registerAction2`). If the module is never imported, it never registers.
Features register themselves on import ... The entry-point imports therefore effectively act as the feature manifest.
